rendered: Short answer: the authors did not run the cathode separation at room temperature. The separation was run hot. Room temperature appears only as a comparison case and as a cooling step after separation. The PVDF binder dissolves in Cyrene only at elevated temperature, and the authors conclude that the separation "should be kept above that temperature" (about ~90 °C[1]), so the process must stay hot to keep PVDF in solution.[2] Running the separation at room temperature was used to show the problem. Filtering the cathode at room temperature left PVDF on the powder, so the FTIR spectrum showed the PVDF band at 871 cm^−1[3], and the authors attribute this to "the reprecipitation of PVDF along with the cathode particles after" cooling to room temperature. The hot-filtered powder lacked that band.[4][5] Room temperature is used later in the process, where the hot supernatant is cooled to room temperature to induce phase separation, so that PVDF/CB composites and recycled Cyrene can be filtered out.[6]
